newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslav opposition unifies behind economist. [CORRECTED 22:17 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Yugoslav opposition unifies behind economist. [CORRECTED 22:17 GMT]

text.p: Rump Yugoslavia's popular former central bank chief, Dragoslav Avramovic, said on Sunday he would lead a united coalition of opposition parties against the ruling Socialists in November general elections.

Avramovic, who became a folk hero for halting a bout of rampant hyperinflation two years ago, told a news conference he had agreed to head the coalition because the current "regime" was blocking desperately needed economic and political reforms.
"I took this job against my wife's wishes," said the 78-year old economist.
"I took it because I am convinced that the enormous changes that began here cannot be maintained in this essentially feudal system."
Avramovic, a former World Bank economist, was sacked as central bank governor in May after losing a battle with government ministers over economic policy.
His calls for fiscal discipline and free market reforms threatened the political and economic monopoly enjoyed by the ruling Socialist party led by Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic.

"I don't see that there will be any change under the present regime, and, in order to get the change which is absolutely necessary, we need to have a change in the political complexion of this country," Avramovic told reporters.

Avramovic said the coalition had three basic goals: to liberalise the state-run economy, to enact Western-style democratic reforms and reduce the size of the central government ruling the Yugoslav republics of Serbia and Montenegro.
Four main opposition parties, which have spent the past several months quarrelling, managed to agree a coalition over the weekend with Avramovic as its top candidate.
Opposition party leaders were clearly buoyed by Avramovic's decision, hoping to capitalise on his reputation as a plain-spoken advocate of the common man.
Belgrade analysts said the Socialists, along with their allies in the United Yugoslav Left and New Democracy, were still expected to emerge victorious in the November 3 vote.
But the coalition led by Avramovic made life more complicated for the Socialists and analysts said the ruling party and its allies were no longer assured of a two-thirds parliamentary majority.
A two-thirds majority would permit the Socialists to amend the constitution, paving the way for Milosevic to become federal president.

The "Together" coalition is comprised of the Serbian Renewal Movement led by Vuk Draskovic, the Civic Alliance led by Vesna Pesic, the Democratic Party led by Zoran Djindjic and the Democratic Party of Serbia (DSS) led by Vojislav Kostunica.
Kostunica, leader of the nationalist DSS, decided to join the coalition on Saturday night after the parties worked out a power-sharing formula for the elections.
Opposition leaders said they signed an agreement which set out the share of parliamentary seats allocated to each coalition member, regardless of election results.
The coalition proposed Avramovic as a potential candidate for federal prime minister or central bank governor.
The ultra-nationalist Serbian Radical Party was the only major opposition faction to stay out of the coalition.
A representative from the organisation of independent trade unions also attended the Belgrade news conference, pledging union support for the coalition.
The participation of trade and farmers' unions showed the coalition represented a very broad movement, Avramovic said.
